specPoints.text: describe how a chain reaction can be set up if the neutrons produced by one fission strike other U-235 nuclei
describe the role played by the control rods and moderator in the fission process
understand the role of shielding around a nuclear reactor

primer.text: A reactor is fission kept on a leash: neutrons from each split find fresh U-235 nuclei and the chain keeps turning, control rods meter how many neutrons survive, the moderator slows them to the speed that splits uranium efficiently, and thick steel-and-concrete shielding soaks up the radiation so workers outside stay safe.

lessons.title: Chain reactions
lessons.opening: One neutron induces a fission, and that fission releases two or three neutrons — each free to strike another U-235 nucleus and split it in turn. That self-feeding sequence is a chain reaction, and if the fissile material exceeds its critical mass the reaction accelerates into an uncontrolled release.
keyPoints: Neutrons from one fission can strike other U-235 nuclei and trigger more fissions.
A chain reaction continues because each split hands neutrons on to the next generation.
One induced fission needs a single neutron but releases two or three.
Above the critical mass of fissile material the reaction rate accelerates uncontrollably.

low.restatement: One neutron in, two-or-three out: the surplus neutrons feed the next splits.
low.analogy: Popcorn popping: each bursting kernel flicks others hot enough to burst, and the pan goes from one pop to many in seconds.
low.examPointer: Chain-reaction diagrams want neutrons drawn striking further U-235 nuclei — clarity beats artwork.

medium.restatement: The neutron census grows 1 → 2–3 → 4–9 → …, so above the critical mass the fission rate compounds without bound.
medium.analogy: A rumour where every listener retells it to two friends — the audience doubles each round until the whole school has heard it.
medium.examPointer: Generation-counting questions are just powers of two — write the sequence out rather than jumping to the answer.

check.stem: A chain reaction keeps going because neutrons from one fission…

options.text: strike other uranium-235 nuclei and split them in turn
options.explanation: Each emitted neutron can seed the next fission.

options.text: are all absorbed by the moderator
options.explanation: The moderator slows neutrons; it does not end the chain.

options.text: fuse with each other into helium
options.explanation: Fusion of neutrons does not happen here.
Escaping neutrons end chains locally; they do not sustain them.

check.stem: How many neutrons enter one induced fission, and how many leave?

options.text: one enters and two or three leave
options.explanation: The split needs a single neutron and releases two or three.
The neutron count grows at each split, not shrinks.
Something must induce the split.
Only one neutron is needed to induce each fission.

check.stem: The critical mass is…

options.text: the minimum amount of fissile material that keeps a chain reaction going
options.explanation: Below it the chain dies out; above it the reaction accelerates.

options.text: the mass of the control rods
options.explanation: Control-rod mass has nothing to do with the definition.

options.text: the mass of uranium that always explodes
options.explanation: Above critical mass the rate can run away — but the term means the threshold.

options.text: the mass of the shielding wall
options.explanation: Shielding mass is a separate design quantity.

check.stem: If the fissile material exceeds the critical mass, the reaction…

options.text: accelerates and can release energy in an uncontrolled explosion
options.explanation: More material means more neutrons find targets faster.
That is what happens below the threshold.
Unchecked, the rate grows rather than holding steady.
Fission chains do not turn into fusion.

check.stem: Why do reactor designers control the chain reaction?

options.text: to hold the fission rate at the level that produces energy safely
options.explanation: Controlled rate means steady power without runaway growth.

options.text: to stop every neutron from moving
options.explanation: Neutrons must keep moving to sustain power.

options.text: to make the reaction grow explosively
options.explanation: Explosive growth is exactly what control prevents.

options.text: to convert the reactor into a weapon
options.explanation: Civil reactors are designed to avoid that regime.

check.stem: Describe how one fission leads to another in uranium.
check.modelAnswer: Each fission releases two or three neutrons, and one of these can strike another U-235 nucleus and split it in its turn.

check.stem: State what happens when the fissile mass exceeds the critical mass.
check.modelAnswer: The rate of fission accelerates, and the energy release can become an uncontrolled explosion.

check.stem: Explain why a chain reaction can grow so quickly once started.
check.modelAnswer: Every split multiplies the neutron supply: one fission emits two or three neutrons, each able to trigger another split, so the number of reactions can double and double again — one split becomes two, then four, then eight.

check.stem: Starting from one induced fission, how many neutrons are released by the third generation if each split releases exactly two and every neutron finds a target?
check.modelAnswer: Generation 1: 1 split → 2 neutrons. Generation 2: 2 splits → 4 neutrons. Generation 3: 4 splits → 8 neutrons. The splits so far number 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

lessons.title: Control rods and the moderator
lessons.opening: A running reactor must hold both the number of free neutrons and their energy in check. Control rods made of neutron-absorbing material are lowered or raised to set the fission rate, while the moderator slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that react efficiently with the uranium fuel; in normal running exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause the next.
keyPoints: Control rods absorb neutrons so the chain reaction runs at a steady, chosen rate.
Lowering the rods absorbs more neutrons and slows fission; raising them lets fission speed up.
The moderator slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that split uranium efficiently.
In normal running, exactly one neutron from each fission causes the next fission.
For an emergency shutdown the rods drop fully in and the reactions stop.

low.restatement: Rods ration the neutrons; the moderator slows them so each one counts.
low.analogy: A turnstile and a walking pace: the rods admit only so many visitors per minute, and the moderator makes sure each walks slowly enough to buy a ticket.
low.examPointer: Two-component questions want both roles named — rods absorb, moderator slows. Mixing them loses the marks.

medium.restatement: Steady power means one neutron per fission seeds the next; rods trim the surplus and the moderator tunes the speed for efficient capture.
medium.analogy: Cruise control: the rods are the brake pedal, the moderator the gear that keeps the engine in its efficient band.
medium.examPointer: Shutdown = rods fully in; rate-up = rods raised; rate-down = rods lowered. Learn the three rod positions.

check.stem: The job of the control rods is to…

options.text: absorb neutrons to regulate the fission rate
options.explanation: Rod depth sets how many neutrons survive to cause fissions.
Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job.
That is the shielding's job.
Heat comes from fission; rods do not heat anything.

check.stem: Raising the control rods makes fission…

options.text: faster, because fewer neutrons are absorbed
options.explanation: Less rod in the core means more free neutrons.

options.text: slower, because more neutrons are absorbed
options.explanation: That is what lowering does.
Rod depth is the rate control.
Fission continues; only full insertion stops it.

check.stem: What is the job of the moderator?

options.text: slow neutrons until they react efficiently with the uranium fuel
options.explanation: Thermal neutrons are far better at inducing fission.
Absorption is the control rods' role.
Gamma absorption belongs to shielding.
Turbines are driven by coolant, not the moderator.

check.stem: Thermal neutrons are neutrons that…

options.text: have slowed to the moderator's temperature and react efficiently with U-235
options.explanation: Collisions with moderator molecules bleed off their momentum.

options.text: carry extra heat to the coolant
options.explanation: Heat transport is the coolant's job.

options.text: are absorbed by the steel wall
options.explanation: Steel shielding is outside the core.
Thermal neutrons are precisely the efficient fission-causers.

check.stem: How is a reactor shut down in an emergency?

options.text: the control rods drop fully in and absorb enough neutrons to stop the chain
options.explanation: Full insertion removes the neutrons the chain needs.
Shutdown is done with the rods, not by draining the moderator.

options.text: the shielding is opened to let radiation out
options.explanation: Shielding never opens during operation.

options.text: the fuel rods are cooled faster
options.explanation: Cooling changes temperature, not the chain rate.

check.stem: State the purpose of the control rods.
check.modelAnswer: Control rods absorb neutrons, and their depth in the core sets how fast the chain reaction runs.

check.stem: State the purpose of the moderator.
check.modelAnswer: The moderator slows the fast fission neutrons so they can split uranium nuclei efficiently.

check.stem: Explain why slowing neutrons helps a reactor keep fission going.
check.modelAnswer: Fast fission neutrons tend to pass uranium nuclei without splitting them; slowed to thermal speeds they interact far more readily, so each neutron is much more likely to be absorbed and induce the next fission.

check.stem: A reactor is producing too much power. Should operators raise or lower the control rods, and why?
check.modelAnswer: They lower the rods: deeper rods absorb more neutrons, so fewer fissions occur each second and the power output falls.

lessons.title: Shielding the reactor
lessons.opening: Everything that leaves a fission is hazardous: the daughter nuclei and the emitted neutrons are radioactive. So the entire reactor is wrapped in shielding — a steel and concrete wall nearly two metres thick that absorbs the emissions and keeps the environment around the reactor safe for workers.
keyPoints: Shielding surrounds the whole reactor and absorbs its hazardous radiation.
The daughter nuclei formed in fission, and the neutrons emitted, are radioactive.
A steel and concrete wall close to two metres thick keeps the surroundings safe for workers.

low.restatement: Thick steel and concrete soak up the reactor's radiation so nobody outside is exposed.
low.analogy: A lead-lined apron at the dentist, scaled up to a wall that wraps the whole machine.
low.examPointer: Quote the thickness as 'nearly two metres' and the materials as steel and concrete — both attract marks.

medium.restatement: Fission products stay radioactive after the split, so the absorbing wall is the last line between the core and the workforce.
medium.analogy: A soundproofed rehearsal room: the noise (radiation) stays inside because the walls (steel and concrete) absorb it before it reaches the corridor.
medium.examPointer: Tie shielding to the radioactivity of daughters and neutrons — the causal chain earns the explanation mark.

check.stem: Shielding around a reactor exists to…

options.text: absorb hazardous radiation so the area outside stays safe
options.explanation: The wall soaks up the reactor's emissions.

options.text: slow neutrons for the chain reaction
options.explanation: That is the moderator's role inside the core.

options.text: absorb neutrons to control the rate
options.explanation: That is the control rods' role.
Cooling is the coolant's job.

check.stem: Which materials form the shielding wall?

options.explanation: The of-record shielding combination is steel plus concrete.
Neither is dense enough for reactor shielding.
Not the materials used for reactor shielding.
Neither forms the surrounding wall.

check.stem: Why are the fission daughter nuclei a hazard inside the core?

options.text: they are radioactive and keep emitting radiation
options.explanation: Radioactive daughters would irradiate the surroundings unshielded.
Magnetism is not the hazard.
Mass is irrelevant to the radiological hazard.
They persist and keep decaying.

check.stem: The steel-and-concrete shielding wall can be nearly…

options.explanation: The of-record thickness is close to two metres.
Two centimetres would barely slow the radiation.
An order of magnitude too thin.
That overstates the design by ten times.

check.stem: Who is directly protected by the shielding?

options.explanation: The wall keeps the environment safe for people outside it.
Shielding protects people, not the fuel.
Rods are inside the core, not protected by the wall.
The shielding's stated purpose is worker safety around the reactor.

check.stem: State the purpose of shielding around a nuclear reactor.
check.modelAnswer: Shielding absorbs the hazardous radiation from the reactor so the environment around it is safe for workers.

check.stem: Name the two materials that make up reactor shielding.
check.modelAnswer: Steel and concrete, in a wall nearly two metres thick.

check.stem: Explain why shielding must surround the reactor even though the fuel sits inside the core.
check.modelAnswer: The fission daughters and emitted neutrons are radioactive, so without a thick absorbing wall their radiation would reach people outside; the steel-and-concrete shielding absorbs those emissions instead.

check.stem: A trainee proposes building the shielding from a 5 cm steel sheet. Give two reasons the plan fails.
check.modelAnswer: The of-record wall is steel plus concrete close to two metres thick; 5 cm (0.05 m) is far too thin and single-material, so far too much radiation would pass through to keep workers safe.

glossary.definition: A self-feeding sequence in which neutrons from each fission trigger further fissions.
The minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain a chain reaction.
Neutron-absorbing rods whose depth in the core sets the fission rate.
Material that slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that split uranium efficiently.
Steel-and-concrete wall, nearly two metres thick, that absorbs the reactor's hazardous radiation.

workedExample.prompt: Complete the chain-reaction diagram for uranium-235: how does the drawing show the reaction spreading?
steps: Draw the released neutrons striking further U-235 nuclei — it is the neutron strikes that cause the next fissions.
Show each struck nucleus splitting and releasing two or more neutrons of its own.
With each generation the neutron count rises, so more and more fissions follow.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The chain spreads generation by generation: each fission needs one neutron and releases two or more, so the number of reactions keeps growing.
